query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1), controlled low-level hydrogen charging—when performed with precise in situ hydrogen concentration monitoring to avoid embrittlement—reduces the local stacking fault energy during deformation, thus promoting the formation of nanoscale twins that reinforce interlamellar interfaces and arrest microcrack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with inherent internal boundaries vulnerable to crack initiation under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Electrochemical hydrogen charging in a dilute acid electrolyte at a moderate hydrogen potential with an in situ hydrogen concentration monitoring system to maintain hydrogen levels within a narrow window that promotes nanotwinning without causing hydrogen embrittlement.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation tests following hydrogen charging; precise control of hydrogen concentration below the threshold for embrittlement, using a tailored electrochemical setup with continuous monitoring.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a high density of in situ nanoscale twins and enhanced interlamellar interface cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Hydrogen reduces the stacking fault energy locally during deformation, triggering the formation of nanotwins. These twins serve as barriers to dislocation motion and act to deflect and arrest propagating microcracks, thereby increasing work hardening and delaying catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the hydrogen-charged specimen is expected to exhibit increased tensile yield strength and enhanced ductility due to improved load distribution, increased work-hardening capacity, and mitigated microcrack propagation.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with conventional dual-phase lamellar colonies that shows limited ductility and susceptibility to microcracking under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only when hydrogen concentration is maintained within an optimal, low-level window. Exceeding this range may lead to hydrogen embrittlement and counteract the desired improvements in mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise quantitative window for hydrogen concentration, the optimal nanotwin density needed for maximal property enhancement, and the scalability of the in situ monitoring technique across different alloy compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set subjected to the controlled hydrogen charging with in situ monitoring and one unmodified control. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests alongside microstructural characterization (e.g., transmission electron microscopy) to quantify nanotwin density and interface integrity.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Nanotwin density and interlamellar interface characterization via TEM/ECCI
Hydrogen concentration profile across the sample thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hydrogen-charged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and ductility relative to the control, or if the expected increase in nanotwin density and interface cohesion is not observed, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 2 shows the tensile deformation behavior of different materials including the CoCrFeMnNi HEA under various in-situ hydrogen charging conditions (Supplementary Fig. 1). Figure 2a reveals that the alloy Inconel 718 (56Ni-18Fe-18Cr-5Nb-3Mo), a benchmark material for tolerance against hydrogen embrittlement, shows significant decrease in both strength and ductility after hydrogen charging. The AISI 310 stainless steel (55Fe-25Cr-20Ni) shows an increase in ultimate strength but a decrease in total elongation when exposed to hydrogen (Fig. 1b). It has also been reported that hydrogen could be controlled to increase the ductility and yet reduce the flow stress of some intermetallic-based titanium alloys. In line with these well studied example alloys literature confirms that the hydrogen induced decrease of strength and/or ductility are characteristic features common to metallic alloys while the simultaneous increase in both, strength and ductility has not been observed before. The CoCrFeMnNi HEA studied here shows exactly this opposite trend when exposed to hydrogen as demonstrated in Fig. 1c,d. Since hydrogenation in the present study was conducted by cathodic charging in alkaline solution and the tensile tests were performed under in-situ hydrogen charging conditions, a gradient in hydrogen concentration from the edge to the inner regions of the samples could have been induced according to previous studies on hydrogen embrittlement of other materials. For this reason associated with the charging process, the intergranular fracture feature observed in the edges is attributed to the high hydrogen concentration near the edges of the samples during the tensile testing in alkaline solution. The fracture mode of microvoid coalescence in the inner regions suggests lower hydrogen concentration in these zones. We also observe that the very fine (<1 μm) ductile dimples in the inner regions of the fracture surface in the hydrogen alloyed samples (Figs. 3b,c and d) occur much more frequently compared to the reference alloy without hydrogen (Fig. 3a). This might be related to the more extensively occurring nanotwinning in the hydrogen alloyed HEAs discussed below.

To reveal the micro-mechanisms behind the hydrogen induced joint increase in both, strength and ductility, we probed the deformation microstructures in the cross-sections of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples tensile tested under various hydrogen charging conditions. Figure 4 shows the typical ECC images of the microstructure near the fracture surfaces of the HEAs samples both with and without hydrogen charging. A few deformation nanotwins in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA sample without hydrogen were observed (Fig. 4a), which is consistent with a previous study which showed that deformation twining can occur in this HEA at relatively high strain levels at room temperature. Interestingly, we observe that the density of nanotwins in the hydrogen alloyed HEA sample significantly increased compared to the hydrogen free alloy (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. 5). For instance, as shown in Fig. 4b, the sample with a diffusible hydrogen concentration of 15.22 wt.ppm (72 h pre-charged at a current density of 25 mA·cm−2) shows a very high density of nanotwins compared to the HEA without hydrogen. We reveal the nanotwinning here by ECCI analysis using bulk samples to avoid any thin slice size and related effects

The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA has a relatively low intrinsic stacking fault energy (~19 mJ·m2), which explains the occurrence of mechanical twinning at room temperature without hydrogen charging. The strong increase in twinning density in the hydrogen alloyed HEA samples reveals that hydrogen reduces the stacking fault energy of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA. This is consistent with the previous studies on the effect of hydrogen on the stacking fault energy in other f.c.c. structured alloys, . Moreover, no other phase formed during the in-situ tensile testing with hydrogen charging according to the XRD results shown in Supplementary Fig. 6. These results also show that the increase in the density of nanotwins that we observe in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA leads to an associated increase in work hardening (Supplementary Fig. 3), which postpones the formation of geometric instabilities to higher strain values, thereby increasing strength and ductility simultaneously.

The beneficial influence of nanotwins on strain hardening is commonly attributed to the “dynamic Hall-Petch” effect, i.e. the formation of nanotwins leads to continuous grain fragmentation by the introduction of new interfaces which effectively reduces the dislocation mean free path, hence, causing further strengthening, . Consistent with this, the strength and ductility of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA increased with the increase in the twinning density caused by the enhanced hydrogen concentration. However, during in-situ tensile testing, unfavorable mechanism caused by hydrogen may also become more significant with higher hydrogen concentration. For instance, hydrogen enhanced localized plasticity can occur in materials that are prone to planar slip, such as the here studied CoCrFeMnNi HEA. This unfavorable mechanism was also observed in a gaseous hydrogen charged CoCrFeMnNi HEA. Thus, a competition may exist between the beneficial nanotwining on the one hand and the unfavorable hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms on the other hand during deformation of the hydrogen charged HEA samples. The appearance of twins close to B2 precipitates here plays a crucial role in offsetting this problem, via the mitigation and accommodation of high fcc-B2 interfacial stresses to prolong strain hardening due to limited plasticity of B2 precipitates (). The twin boundaries reduce the dislocation mean free path, thus sustaining strain hardening to delay the onset of fracture. This phenomenon is referred to as the “dynamic Hall-Petch” effect (). The increase in yield strength at a lower temperature (77 K) means that critical twinning stress is easily reached because of the relative temperature insensitivity of twinning stress, and thus, nanotwinning occurs at relatively lower strains (). This improves the SHR and delays failure at 77 K, even in the presence of the B2 phase that usually causes strong embrittlement problems at cryogenic temperature. proposals.material_system: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies, for example an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy
proposals.intervention: Introduce controlled hydrogen charging (via electrochemical treatment) to achieve an optimal, low concentration of interstitial hydrogen
proposals.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation after hydrogen charging performed at a controlled, moderate hydrogen potential in a dilute acid electrolyte; ensure hydrogen concentration is below levels that cause conventional embrittlement
proposals.structural_mediator: Increased formation of nano-scale twins and enhanced interlamellar interface cohesion
proposals.mechanism: Hydrogen reduces the stacking-fault energy locally in both lamellar phases, promoting in situ nanotwinning during deformation. These twins act to deflect and arrest microcrack propagation along the internal boundaries, while their presence also increases work-hardening and delays crack coalescence.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the hydrogen-charged alloy is expected to show an increase in tensile yield strength and a significant enhancement in room-temperature ductility because the nanostructural twin networks improve load transfer and mitigate catastrophic microcrack growth.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention directly targets the deleterious role of internal lamellae boundaries—by promoting nanotwinning and strengthening the interfaces, hydrogen charging can arrest microcrack initiation and propagation while also providing an in situ mechanism for additional work-hardening, thereby simultaneously improving both strength and ductility.

critiques.addresses_problem: The hypothesis directly targets the primary issue by aiming to strengthen interlamellar interfaces and inhibit microcrack initiation via in situ nanotwinning, which is the critical microstructural weakness in eutectic high‐entropy alloys.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraints by specifying operation on a representative eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1), at room-temperature tensile deformation, with controlled hydrogen charging in a dilute acid electrolyte. However, it requires very precise control of hydrogen concentration to avoid crossing into embrittlement territory.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound: the reduction of local stacking-fault energy by low-level hydrogen charging to promote nanotwinning is well-documented in similar f.c.c. HEA systems and can, in principle, improve both strength and ductility by deflecting microcrack propagation and enhancing work hardening.
critiques.feasibility: The proposed intervention is feasible using established electrochemical hydrogen charging methods and routine tensile deformation tests. Nanotwin detection can be accomplished through electron microscopy, which is standard in materials research.
critiques.evidence: Multiple records (e.g., PMC5575320::web::008, PMC5575320::web::010, PMC5575320::web::009, and PMC8378815::web::012) support the beneficial effect of controlled hydrogen charging in promoting nanotwinning and improving mechanical properties in HEAs. There is also evidence that excessive hydrogen can be detrimental, so careful control is critical.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk lies in the possibility of overcharging with hydrogen, which could lead to localized high hydrogen concentrations and activate hydrogen embrittlement or hydrogen enhanced localized plasticity, ultimately triggering premature microcracking.
critiques.fix: Implement a precise, in-situ hydrogen concentration monitoring and control scheme during electrochemical charging to ensure that the hydrogen levels remain within the narrow optimal window that promotes nanotwinning without causing embrittlement.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly addresses the challenge of simultaneously increasing strength and ductility by targeting the weak interlamellar boundaries through in situ nanotwinning induced by controlled hydrogen charging. The critic’s review supports the mechanism but emphasizes the need for precise hydrogen concentration control to avoid embrittlement. This fix—implementing an in situ hydrogen concentration monitoring scheme—is both feasible and grounded in multiple records that document the beneficial effects of low-level hydrogen charging. Thus, we adopt direction A with the recommended modification.
